teaching.text: A **mass-spring system** vibrates because the spring pulls the mass toward **equilibrium**, while the mass keeps moving. Equilibrium is the resting position toward which the spring pulls.
children: Pull the mass away from equilibrium and release it. The stretched spring pulls it back. The mass is still moving when it reaches equilibrium, so it passes that point and the spring pushes it back from the other side.
The **m** inside the moving object stands for its mass. The guide through the middle marks **equilibrium**, the reference position from which it moves away and returns.

teaching.text: **Longitudinal motion** runs along the spring, so the mass moves left and right. **Transverse motion** runs across the line between the supports, so the mass moves up and down.
children: The drawings show the same repeating pattern in two directions. The transverse springs pull the displaced mass back toward the middle, and its continued motion carries it through the middle.

teaching.text: **Frequency** counts complete back-and-forth cycles in a second. The **Reference** row is the starting condition used for both comparisons. Its mass is labeled **m**, and its total restoring stiffness is labeled **K**.
In the **Bigger mass** row, **4m means four times the reference mass**, while K stays unchanged. The heavier mass is harder to turn around, so each cycle takes longer.
children: **Half the rate** means half as many cycles in the same time as the reference. It describes slower repetition, rather than a smaller movement.

teaching.text: In the **Stiffer spring** row, the mass stays at m and **4K means four times the reference stiffness**. The stronger restoring pull turns the mass around sooner.
children: **Twice the rate** means twice as many cycles in the same time as the reference. This is a higher frequency.

teaching.text: The left and right columns show **longitudinal** and **transverse** motion, along and across the spring line. Within each row their frequencies match. Changing the direction of the drawing does not change the effects of mass and stiffness.

explained: one changed property at a time

teaching.text: A **mode** is a particular pattern of vibration of the whole system. The two equal masses and three springs can move in **two modes**. The numbers **1 and 2 on the objects identify the two masses**. The row labels **mode 1 and mode 2 identify whole-system patterns**.
In **mode 1**, both masses move together. They both rise and fall in the transverse drawing, or both move left and right in the longitudinal drawing.
children: The middle spring moves with them without stretching or compressing. The outer springs provide the restoring pull.
The dashed marks show each mass’s **equilibrium position**. Moving together means both move to the same side of those positions at the same time.

teaching.text: In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. When one rises, the other falls. In the longitudinal drawing, they move toward and away from each other.
children: The middle spring now stretches and compresses as well. More stiffness takes part in the motion, so **mode 2 has a higher frequency than mode 1**. The springs themselves have not been replaced or stiffened.

teaching.text: **Both modes can occur at the same time.** Lifting both masses but making one higher than the other starts a combination of moving together and moving against each other. The combined movement is a mixture of the two modes.
children: The **Both modes** row adds the motions of mode 1 and mode 2. Its more complicated movement still contains the two original frequencies.

teaching.text: A system with **three masses has three modes**. Each mode specifies how all three masses move in relation to one another.
children: The object numbers **1, 2 and 3** identify the left, middle and right masses. The **mode numbers** label different ways all three masses move, rather than assigning one mode to each mass.

teaching.text: In **mode 1**, all three masses move in the same direction. This is the lowest-frequency pattern because the neighboring masses move mostly together, with relatively little stretching between them.
In **mode 2**, the middle mass stays still while the two outer masses move against each other. One outer mass goes up as the other goes down, or they move left and right in opposite directions.
In **mode 3**, the middle mass moves against both outer masses. The outer masses move together in one direction while the middle mass moves in the other.
children: This creates the most stretching and compression between neighbors, so mode 3 has the highest frequency.

teaching.text: The three modes can also occur **together**. Their motions add to produce the combined movement in the bottom row.
children: The **All three** row combines modes 1, 2 and 3, so it contains three mode frequencies. It does not introduce a fourth mode.

teaching.text: For these chains, **N masses give N modes**. N means the number of masses. A two-mass chain has two modes, and a six-mass chain has six.
children: The **rows count masses**, from one to six. The **columns count modes** within each chain. N is a count of masses, rather than the mass of one object.

teaching.text: The lowest mode has the masses moving together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: In the second mode, the left and right parts move in opposite directions. With an odd number of masses, the middle mass stays still.
More motion against neighboring parts creates more stretching and compression, so the higher modes have higher frequencies.
Moving right within one row compares different modes of the **same chain**. Moving down one column compares the same kind of pattern across chains with different numbers of masses.

teaching.text: A **string** has mass and springiness throughout its length. Treating it as many small connected masses and springs explains how it can support the same kinds of vibration patterns.
children: The modes of a chain with separate masses are not generally exact whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** cannot move at either end. Its first mode has one moving section. The second has two sections moving against each other, and the third has three.
The mode frequencies are **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**. The second mode vibrates twice as fast as the first, and the third vibrates three times as fast.
children: **Hertz**, abbreviated Hz, means cycles per second.

Here **100 Hz** is the base frequency, or 100 cycles per second. The **200 Hz** second mode completes two cycles while the first completes one. The displayed motion is slowed so these patterns can be seen.

teaching.text: Several modes can vibrate at once. The combined string adds their motions at each point, producing a more complex shape.

A **spectrum** shows the frequencies present and the strength of each one. **Frequency in Hz runs left to right**, and **amplitude runs upward**. A spike’s position gives its rate, while its height gives how strongly it contributes.
children: With five modes present, there are five spikes. With only the third mode present, there is one spike at that mode’s frequency.
The black dot marks the **pickup point**, where motion is measured. The five equal-height spikes are a chosen setting at that point, rather than five equal frequencies.

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a surface that can vibrate. Its moving parts extend in two directions, so its modes divide the surface into regions rather than dividing only a line.
children: The first mode rises and falls as one region. Other modes have neighboring regions moving against one another, with still lines between them.

The pair **(1, 1)** means one moving region in each direction. **(2, 1)** divides one direction into two regions, **(1, 2)** divides the other, and **(2, 2)** has two in each direction, making four alternating regions.

teaching.text: Several modes can occur together. Their motions add to make the changing surface shown in the combined panel.
children: The spectrum shows a spike for each active frequency. The equally spaced frequencies in this demonstration are assigned for illustration, rather than calculated as the natural frequencies of this rectangle.

The **All 5 modes** panel adds the five patterns. The black **pickup point** identifies where that combined motion is measured. In the spectrum, horizontal position gives **frequency in Hz** and vertical height gives **relative amplitude**.

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** are vibrating tissue with many moving parts. Describing their motion in modes connects that movement with the frequencies present in a voice.

A **fixed–free system** has one end that stays still and one end that can move. A **node** is a location that stays still throughout the vibration. An **antinode** is a location with the greatest motion.
children: Each pattern has a node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end.
The **fixed bottom** stays in place, and the **free top** can move. These boundary labels apply to every mode, including those with still points inside the system.

teaching.text: The allowed frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency, one, three, five and seven times that frequency.
children: The first mode has no still point inside the string. Higher modes add still points and regions moving against one another while keeping the free end moving.
In the pictured example, mode 1 is **100 Hz** and mode 2 is **300 Hz**. The 2 counts the second allowed pattern; 300 Hz gives its rate of 300 cycles per second.

The spectrum’s peaks at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz** show the odd-multiple pattern. Their positions give different frequencies, while their equal heights show equal contributions in this illustration.

teaching.text: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end makes the lowest frequency **half** that of the fixed–fixed string.
**Stabilization** means reducing fluctuations and keeping a system near **equilibrium**, a stable balance. The economic example concerns swings in unemployment and inflation.
children: The **black line represents unemployment** and the **gray line represents inflation**. Their repeated peaks and troughs show fluctuation; the hands pressing them down represent making those fluctuations smaller.

teaching.text: **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or **DSGE**, names a theory of how an economy changes and responds to unpredictable events.
children: **Dynamic** refers to change over time. **Stochastic** refers to unpredictable shocks. Stabilization policy aims to make the resulting fluctuations smaller.

teaching.text: The spring pulls a displaced mass toward **equilibrium**, its resting position. The mass keeps moving as it reaches that position, passes it and is pushed back from the other side. The result is **vibration**.
children: The **m** inside the moving object stands for its mass. The guide through the middle marks **equilibrium**, the reference position from which it moves away and returns.

teaching.text: In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves left and right along the spring. In **transverse motion**, it moves up and down between the supports.
children: Both drawings show a restoring pull together with the mass’s continued motion. Changing the drawing’s direction does not change that explanation.

teaching.text: **Frequency** counts complete back-and-forth cycles in a second. The **Reference** row is the starting condition used for both comparisons. Its mass is labeled **m**, and its total restoring stiffness is labeled **K**.
In the **Bigger mass** row, **4m means four times the reference mass**, while K stays unchanged. The heavier mass is harder to turn around, so each cycle takes longer.
children: **Half the rate** means half as many cycles in the same time as the reference. It describes slower repetition, rather than a smaller movement.

teaching.text: In the **Stiffer spring** row, the mass stays at m and **4K means four times the reference stiffness**. The stronger restoring pull turns the mass around sooner.
children: **Twice the rate** means twice as many cycles in the same time as the reference. This is a higher frequency.

teaching.text: The left and right columns show **longitudinal** and **transverse** motion, along and across the spring line. Within each row their frequencies match. Changing the direction of the drawing does not change the effects of mass and stiffness.

explained: one changed property at a time

teaching.text: The two masses have **two modes**, or patterns of vibration. Both masses participate in either mode. The numbers **1 and 2 on the objects identify the two masses**. The row labels **mode 1 and mode 2 identify whole-system patterns**.
In **mode 1**, the masses move together. The middle spring moves with them without stretching or compressing, so the outer springs supply the restoring pull.
children: The dashed marks show each mass’s **equilibrium position**. Moving together means both move to the same side of those positions at the same time.

teaching.text: In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. The middle spring stretches and compresses as well as the outer springs.
children: The extra contribution from the middle spring makes the system effectively stiffer in mode 2. **Mode 2 therefore has a higher frequency**, even though the same masses and springs are present in both modes.

teaching.text: Lifting both masses to different heights starts **both modes together**. The bottom row combines their motions rather than adding a new mode.
children: The **Both modes** row adds the motions of mode 1 and mode 2. Its more complicated movement still contains the two original frequencies.

teaching.text: The three masses have **three modes**. In mode 1, all three move together. In mode 2, the middle mass stays still while the outer masses move against each other. In mode 3, the middle mass moves against both outer masses.
children: The object numbers **1, 2 and 3** identify the left, middle and right masses. The **mode numbers** label different ways all three masses move, rather than assigning one mode to each mass.
The **All three** row adds those three patterns. The three colors keep the same mass identities as the motion changes.

teaching.text: A change in a spring’s **stiffness** matters when that spring stretches or compresses in the pattern being examined.
children: Stiffening a middle spring has little effect on a pattern that hardly stretches it. It raises the frequency of a pattern that does stretch it.

teaching.text: Making the **middle mass heavier** lowers the frequencies of modes 1 and 3, because the middle mass moves in those modes.
children: Mode 2 stays unchanged because its middle mass does not move. Mode 3 is affected more strongly than mode 1 because the middle mass moves more in that pattern.

teaching.text: **N masses give N modes** in these chains. The first mode moves the masses together. The second divides them into two opposing regions, and the third has the middle region moving against the sides.
children: Higher modes involve more stretching between neighboring parts and have higher frequencies.
The **rows count masses**, from one to six. The **columns count modes** within each chain. N is a count of masses, rather than the mass of one object.

teaching.text: A **string** has both mass and springiness along its length. A chain with more and more connected masses and springs approaches that continuous system.
children: Moving right within one row compares different modes of the **same chain**. Moving down one column compares the same kind of pattern across chains with different numbers of masses.

teaching.text: A vibrating string can contain **several modes at once**. Adding those simple patterns produces the complicated movement of the whole string. A **pure tone** contains just one frequency.
The modes of an ideal **fixed–fixed string** have frequencies that are **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**.
children: The **100 Hz** first mode completes 100 cycles per second. The **200 Hz** second mode has twice that rate. These numbers label frequency, while mode 1 and mode 2 label the spatial patterns.

teaching.text: The first mode contains one moving section. The second fits two opposing sections into the same string length, and the third fits three.
children: Fitting more sections into the same length makes the waves shorter and the frequency higher. The second mode vibrates twice as fast as the first, and the third vibrates three times as fast.

teaching.text: The combined string adds the motions of several modes. Its **spectrum** separates that combined motion into frequencies.
children: A spike’s position gives its frequency, and its height gives its amplitude. The equal spike heights are a setting of this demonstration.

The graph places **frequency in Hz horizontally** and **amplitude vertically**. The black dot identifies where the combined string’s motion is measured. Equal spike heights mean equal contributions at that pickup point.

teaching.text: **Increasing mass lowers frequency; increasing stiffness raises it.** The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. The effect depends on what the changed part does in a particular mode.
children: An **up arrow** means an increase, and a **down arrow** means a decrease. Stiffness is written **k** or **K**.
The first printed line has a typo beside stiffness. The stiffness principle below it gives the correct direction, **more stiffness raises frequency**.

teaching.text: Added mass matters most **where there is strong motion**. Adding it at a node, a location that stays still, leaves that mode’s frequency unchanged.
Added stiffness matters **where there is stretching or compression**. Neighboring parts can stretch against one another around a still point even though the point itself does not move.
children: A region can move strongly with little change in spacing between neighboring parts. Strong motion therefore does not mean strong stretching.

teaching.text: The endpoints determine the allowed frequency pattern. A **fixed–fixed string** has whole-number harmonics. A **fixed–free system** has odd multiples of its lowest frequency.
children: In an **n-mass system**, **n** counts the masses and the available modes. Three masses, for example, allow three whole-system vibration patterns. This count differs from **m**, the mass of an individual part.

teaching.text: In the first mode of this fixed–fixed string, the **middle moves most**, while the ends stay still. The middle region moves up and down with little stretching between nearby parts.
children: The rows labeled **mode 1 through mode 5** show different patterns of the same fixed–fixed string. The Hz values identify their vibration rates; they do not measure how far a part moves.

teaching.text: Near a fixed end there is little movement, but neighboring parts stretch against one another. **Strong motion and strong stretching occur in different regions.**
children: Higher modes repeat this alternation at more places along the string. A local change must therefore be matched to the pattern of the mode being examined.
The **black dot** in the combined panel is the location used for the spectrum. That graph separates frequency along the horizontal axis from the strength of each contribution along the vertical axis.

teaching.text: The **green box marks the same location** in two vibration patterns. **Mode 4** has strong motion there, while **mode 5** has strong stretching around a still point. Making that section heavier and stiffer therefore affects the two modes differently.
children: The **400 Hz** and **500 Hz** labels give the example’s starting frequencies for modes 4 and 5. The green box locates the physical change; it is not a frequency range on a spectrum.

teaching.text: In **mode 4**, added mass lowers the frequency because the section moves. Added stiffness has little effect because there is little stretching at that location.
In **mode 5**, added mass has no effect because the marked point stays still. Added stiffness raises the frequency because neighboring parts stretch and compress there.
The combined result is **mode 4 down and mode 5 up**. Predicting the effect of a small local change is called **perturbation**.
children: In the written answer, **m** means mass and **k** means stiffness. Both increase at the marked location, while the rest of the string is unchanged.

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface. Its first mode moves as one region, while higher modes have more regions moving against one another.
children: The two-number labels identify how the surface is divided in its two directions. A pattern with two regions in one direction has those regions moving oppositely.

The pair **(1, 1)** means one moving region in each direction. **(2, 1)** divides one direction into two regions, **(1, 2)** divides the other, and **(2, 2)** has two in each direction, making four alternating regions.

teaching.text: Several membrane modes can occur **at the same time**. Their motions add to make the combined surface, and the spectrum has a spike for each active frequency.
children: The equally spaced frequencies and equal spike heights are assigned for this illustration. They are not a calculation of this rectangle’s natural frequencies.

The **All 5 modes** panel adds the five patterns. The black **pickup point** identifies where that combined motion is measured. In the spectrum, horizontal position gives **frequency in Hz** and vertical height gives **relative amplitude**.

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** contain many connected moving parts, so their vibration can also be described through modes.
In a **fixed–free system**, the fixed end is a **node**, a location with no motion, and the free end is an **antinode**, a location with the greatest motion.
children: The **fixed bottom** stays in place, and the **free top** can move. These boundary labels apply to every mode, including those with still points inside the system.

teaching.text: The frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency. The first mode contains one section from no motion to maximum motion. The second contains three such sections, and the third contains five.
children: The endpoint conditions must stay the same in every mode. This is why the allowed patterns skip the even multiples.
In the pictured example, mode 1 is **100 Hz** and mode 2 is **300 Hz**. The 2 counts the second allowed pattern; 300 Hz gives its rate of 300 cycles per second.

The spectrum’s peaks at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz** show the odd-multiple pattern. Their positions give different frequencies, while their equal heights show equal contributions in this illustration.

teaching.text: The idealized **vocal tract** is closed at the vocal-fold end and open at the lips. Its air has little back-and-forth motion at the closed end and can move freely at the open end.
The air in the **vocal tract** has mass and springiness. Its **inertia** resists changes in motion, and its springiness supplies a restoring effect when it is compressed.
children: The model is fixed at the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds, and free at the lips. The air moves back and forth along the tube.

teaching.text: **F1** and **F2** label the first and second **formants**, the air resonances in the vocal tract. A resonance is a frequency at which that air vibrates strongly. The numbers order the resonances from lowest to highest.
children: In this uniform fixed–free tube, F2 is three times F1. **Mode 2** is the next allowed pattern of the air column; it does not name a second mass.
The marks **1/3** and **2/3** measure distance along the tract **from the glottis toward the lips**. They locate the modeled /a/ and /i/ constrictions; /u/ marks the free lip end.

explained: same air column in two modes

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract. Vowels differ in where the tongue or lips create that narrowing.
children: **High** and **low** describe tongue height. **Front**, **central** and **back** describe its position from front to back.
The **High/Low** and **Front/Back** labels organize tongue positions in the vowel images. They describe where the tongue is, rather than high or low voice pitch.

teaching.text: The high front vowel in **Dean** has a constriction near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. **Dune** has rounding at the lips. **Don** has a constriction near one third of the distance from the glottis.
children: **Done** is the central example with no marked constriction. **Dan** is shown as low and front.
The fractions **1/3** and **2/3** describe distance **from the glottis toward the lips**. A constriction at two thirds is farther toward the front of the tract than one at one third.

teaching.text: The constriction’s **location** matters because the air does different amounts of moving and compressing at different places in each mode.

The same location can behave differently in **mode 1 and mode 2**. Near the lips, both modes have strong motion. Farther inside the tract, one mode can have strong motion where another has strong compression.
children: The upper chain is **mode 1, associated with F1**; the lower is **mode 2, associated with F2**. Both chains represent the same tract, drawn twice to compare its two patterns.

teaching.text: **F1 and F2 are air resonances**, not the harmonics of the vocal folds. A constriction changes a formant according to what the air does at that location in its mode.
children: The /a/ mark is near one third of the distance from the glottis. The /i/ mark is near two thirds, and /u/ marks the lip end.
The **1/3** and **2/3** marks are distances measured from the fixed glottal end toward the open lips. They identify constriction locations, rather than fractions of a formant frequency.

explained: same air column in two modes

teaching.text: For **/u/**, lip rounding narrows the air passage at the **free end**. This increases the effective mass of the air in a region where both modes move strongly.
children: The **larger blue masses at the right-hand end** show the added mass near the lips. The upper and lower rows apply that same change to **mode 1/F1** and **mode 2/F2**.

teaching.text: More mass at a moving location slows a mode. **Both F1 and F2 therefore decrease.** There is little compression at the lip end, so the added stiffness contributes little to the change.
children: The downward arrows in **F1 ↓ and F2 ↓** mean both resonance frequencies decrease. They do not show air flowing downward; the air moves back and forth along the tract.

explained: same local change in two modes

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two thirds of the distance from the glottis**. It increases mass and stiffness at the same location, but the two modes use that location differently.
children: The **highlighted region around the 2/3 mark** locates the modified air in both rows. This fraction is distance from the glottis, while **mode 1/F1** and **mode 2/F2** identify the patterns being compared.

teaching.text: Mode 1 has strong motion there. Added mass slows that vibration, so **F1 decreases**.
children: Mode 2 has strong compression and expansion there. Added stiffness strengthens the restoring action, so **F2 increases**.

In **F1 ↓ and F2 ↑**, the arrows mean the first resonance becomes lower in frequency and the second becomes higher. Both changes result from the same constriction, rather than two separate tongue movements.

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is near **one third of the distance from the glottis**. In mode 1, compression and expansion are strong there, so added stiffness raises **F1**.
children: The **highlighted region near 1/3** is the changed location in both chains. The fraction measures distance from the fixed glottal end, not a third of the frequency.

teaching.text: In mode 2, motion is strong at that location, so added mass lowers **F2**.
children: The result is **F1 up and F2 down**. One narrowing has opposite effects on the two resonances because each mode has a different pattern.

The upper chain shows **mode 1/F1** and the lower shows **mode 2/F2**. In **F1 ↑ and F2 ↓**, the arrows describe resonance frequency increases and decreases, rather than the direction in which air travels.

teaching.text: A local change affects a mode according to **what changes and what that location does**. Added mass lowers frequency when the part moves. Added stiffness raises frequency when neighboring parts stretch or compress.
children: The **up arrow** means an increase, and the **down arrow** means a decrease. **m** names mass, **k or K** names stiffness, and **n** counts the masses in an n-mass system.
The first printed line has a typo beside stiffness. The stiffness principle below it gives the correct direction, **more stiffness raises frequency**.

teaching.text: The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. Raising both at one location does not guarantee cancellation, because their influence depends on the mode.
children: At a still point, more mass has little effect but more stiffness can matter strongly. At a strongly moving location with little stretching, more mass matters most.

In an **n-mass system**, **n** counts the masses and the available modes. Three masses, for example, allow three whole-system vibration patterns. This count differs from **m**, the mass of an individual part.

teaching.text: **Motion** is the back-and-forth travel of a part of the air. **Compression** is the change in spacing between neighboring parts. These are different properties.
children: Lines of air that move together can travel a long way without becoming closer together. Compression occurs when their spacing changes.
The top **Schwa** row shows the uniform-tube vowel. The rows **Mode 1 @ F1**, **Mode 2 @ F2** and **Mode 3 @ F3** separate its three displayed air-motion patterns.
The small blue circles represent groups of air molecules. The closed end is on the **left**, and the open lip end is on the **right**. Each row uses the same tract orientation.

teaching.text: In the first mode, air has little motion near the closed glottal end, where compression is strong. Near the open lips, motion is strongest and compression is weakest.
Higher modes contain more alternating regions of strong motion and strong compression. This lets one constriction affect two formants differently.
children: **F1, F2 and F3** rank the air resonances from lowest to highest. The mode number identifies a pattern, while its formant gives the frequency associated with that pattern.

teaching.text: **More mass lowers frequency; more stiffness raises it.** The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. Raising both does not automatically make their effects cancel.
children: An **up arrow** means an increase, and a **down arrow** means a decrease. Stiffness is written **k** or **K**.
The first printed line has a typo beside stiffness. The stiffness principle below it gives the correct direction, **more stiffness raises frequency**.

teaching.text: The outcome depends on **location within a mode**. At a still point with strong stretching around it, added mass contributes little while added stiffness raises the frequency.
children: At a strongly moving location with little stretching, added mass lowers frequency while added stiffness contributes little.

teaching.text: The same system has several modes, and each uses its parts differently. A prediction must therefore refer to a **particular mode**, rather than to “the frequency” without specifying which one.
children: In an **n-mass system**, **n** counts the masses and the available modes. Three masses, for example, allow three whole-system vibration patterns. This count differs from **m**, the mass of an individual part.

teaching.text: These chains have equal masses and springs, with both ends fixed. **N masses give N modes**, so each row has as many possible patterns as it has masses.
children: The **rows count masses**, from one to six. The **columns count modes** within each chain. N is a count of masses, rather than the mass of one object.

teaching.text: The lowest mode moves the masses together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: More relative movement between neighbors means more stretching and compression, which makes the higher-frequency patterns faster.
Moving right within one row compares different modes of the **same chain**. Moving down one column compares the same kind of pattern across chains with different numbers of masses.

teaching.text: A chain with separate masses does not generally have frequencies that are exact whole-number multiples. The **ideal string** is the continuous system with that harmonic relationship.

A string fixed at both ends must have **no motion at each end**. The first mode contains one **half-wave packet**, a section that runs from a still point through a moving region to another still point.
The second mode fits two half-wave packets into the same length, and the fifth fits five. More packets mean shorter waves and higher frequencies.
children: The second harmonic vibrates at twice the **base frequency**, and the fifth at five times that frequency. These whole-number multiples are **harmonics**.
The **numbered yellow rectangles count half-wave packets** within each pattern. One packet fits the first mode, two fit the second and five fit the fifth, all within the same string length.
The **1×, 2× and 5×** labels compare frequencies with the first mode. The example uses a 100 Hz base, meaning 100 cycles per second, and the higher labels express multiples of that starting rate.

teaching.text: The model of **vocal-fold vibration** predicts harmonics as well. A voice’s base frequency can differ from another’s while the whole-number relationship remains.
A string can vibrate in **several modes at once**. Adding the movement from each mode at every point gives the changing shape of the combined string.
children: The **All 5 modes** panel is the same string with five patterns added together. The black dot marks where that combined motion is measured.

teaching.text: The higher modes repeat more quickly. While the first completes one cycle, the fifth completes five in this harmonic system.
children: The spectrum has one spike for each active frequency. Its equal spike heights are deliberately set for this demonstration, rather than being a requirement for every string sound.

The spectrum uses **frequency in Hz horizontally** and **amplitude vertically**. Here 100 Hz means 100 cycles per second, while the 200 Hz mode repeats twice as fast. Equal spike heights describe equal contributions at the pickup point, rather than equal rates.

teaching.text: A **membrane** extends in two directions. Its mode labels use two numbers to describe the moving regions in those directions.
children: In **(1, 1)**, the surface rises and falls as one region. In **(2, 1)** or **(1, 2)**, two regions move against each other. In **(2, 2)**, four regions alternate, and in **(3, 1)** there are three regions along one direction.
The first and second numbers count regions in the two different directions. They identify the **spatial pattern**, while the separate Hz label gives its frequency.

teaching.text: The combined surface adds these separate motions. Its spectrum shows the active frequencies at the marked pickup point.
children: The harmonic frequencies in this illustration are assigned teaching values. They are not the natural frequencies calculated for the pictured rectangle.

The **All 5 modes** panel adds the five patterns. The black **pickup point** identifies where that combined motion is measured. In the spectrum, horizontal position gives **frequency in Hz** and vertical height gives **relative amplitude**.

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has a **node** at its fixed end and an **antinode** at its free end. A node stays still through the cycle, while an antinode has the greatest motion.
children: The **fixed bottom** stays in place, and the **free top** can move. These boundary labels apply to every mode, including those with still points inside the system.

teaching.text: Its first mode runs from no motion at one end to maximum motion at the other. Higher patterns must keep both endpoint conditions.
children: The allowed frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency, one, three, five and seven times that frequency.
In the pictured example, mode 1 is **100 Hz** and mode 2 is **300 Hz**. The 2 counts the second allowed pattern; 300 Hz gives its rate of 300 cycles per second.

The spectrum’s peaks at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz** show the odd-multiple pattern. Their positions give different frequencies, while their equal heights show equal contributions in this illustration.

teaching.text: For the same length and wave speed, this system has a lowest frequency **half** that of a string fixed at both ends. The idealized air in the vocal tract has fixed–free endpoint conditions.
A **quarter-wave packet** runs from a node, where there is no motion, to an antinode, where motion is greatest. A fixed–free pattern must begin and end in this way.
The allowed modes contain **one, three, five or seven quarter-wave packets**. Adding a pair of packets keeps an antinode at the free end.
children: An even number would put a node at that free end, so it would fail the endpoint condition.
The **yellow rectangles and their numbers count quarter-wave packets**, not separate modes. Each column is one mode, containing one, three, five or seven packets.

teaching.text: More packets within the same length mean shorter waves and a higher frequency. The odd packet counts explain the **odd-multiple frequency pattern**.
Count the **quarter-wave packets** from the fixed bottom to the free top. The first mode contains one packet, the second three, the third five and the fourth seven.
children: Each **yellow box** marks one quarter-wave packet. The numbers run through the boxes within a single mode, so mode 2 contains three numbered packets and mode 4 contains seven.

teaching.text: Each pattern must start at a **node** and end at an **antinode**. The extra packets add still points inside while preserving motion at the free end.
children: The mode number counts allowed patterns. It does not give the multiple of the lowest frequency. The second mode has three times that frequency.

teaching.text: The **vocal tract** contains air that has both mass and springiness. The chain models the air’s **inertia**, its resistance to changes in motion, and its restoring response when compressed.
The model is fixed at the vocal-fold end and free at the lips. Its lowest mode is the **first formant, F1**, and the next is the **second formant, F2**.
children: In a uniform fixed–free tube, the frequencies follow one, three and five times F1. F2 therefore has three times F1’s frequency.
The **1 and 2 in F1 and F2 rank the resonances**. They do not count air particles or say that F2 must be twice F1.

teaching.text: The marked /a/, /i/ and /u/ locations identify where the modeled constrictions act. Their effect depends on how each mode moves or compresses there.
children: The **1/3 /a/** and **2/3 /i/** marks locate distances from the fixed glottal end. The **/u/** mark is at the free lip end. Both rows use the same locations to compare different modes.

explained: same air column in two modes

teaching.text: In the idealized tube, the **vocal-fold end is closed** and the **lip end is open**. Air has little back-and-forth motion at the closed end and its greatest motion near the open end.
children: The top **Schwa** row shows the uniform-tube vowel. The rows **Mode 1 @ F1**, **Mode 2 @ F2** and **Mode 3 @ F3** separate its three displayed air-motion patterns.
The small blue circles represent groups of air molecules. The closed end is on the **left**, and the open lip end is on the **right**. Each row uses the same tract orientation.

teaching.text: The lines represent groups of air molecules. **Changing spacing** between neighboring lines indicates compression and expansion. Lines that travel together without changing spacing show strong motion with little compression.
Mode 1 has no internal motion node. Mode 2 adds one, and mode 3 adds two. Around a node, neighboring air can repeatedly compress and expand even though the node itself stays still.
The resonances are the **formants**, F1, F2 and F3. The uniform fixed–free model has odd-multiple frequencies. Changing the shape of the tract changes those resonances.
Vowels differ in where the tongue and lips create a **constriction**, a narrowing in the vocal tract. **High/low** describes tongue height, and **front/back** describes its location along the tract.
children: The **High/Low** and **Front/Back** labels organize tongue positions in the vowel images. They describe where the tongue is, rather than high or low voice pitch.

teaching.text: The high front vowel in **Dean** has a narrowing near two thirds of the distance from the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds. The low back vowel in **Don** has a narrowing near one third.
children: **Dune** includes lip rounding and a back tongue constriction. **Done** is the central, unmarked-constriction example, while **Dan** is low and front.
The fractions **1/3** and **2/3** describe distance **from the glottis toward the lips**. A constriction at two thirds is farther toward the front of the tract than one at one third.

teaching.text: The location matters because different parts of each mode have different amounts of motion and compression. The modeled lip constriction of **/u/** has a strong effect on the first two formants.

For **/u/**, the back tongue constriction and the lip constriction play different roles. In this account, the back constriction is the example where the effects balance and leave the formants unchanged. The lip constriction lowers the first two formants.
A **constriction** narrows the air passage and raises both its effective **mass** and **stiffness**. These changes tend to affect frequency in opposite directions.
children: The two vocal-tract images compare a more open passage with a **narrowed passage under the tongue**. The arrow indicates that shape change, rather than a direction of particle vibration.

teaching.text: Their effects do not automatically cancel. The result depends on **what the air is doing at the constriction in a particular mode**.
children: At a region with strong motion, added mass matters most and tends to lower that formant.
At a region with strong compression, added stiffness matters most and tends to raise that formant.

teaching.text: The same constriction can therefore lower one formant and raise another. Each mode uses the location differently.
At each location in the air column, distinguish **movement of the air** from **change in spacing between neighboring parts**. The second is compression and expansion.
children: The top **Schwa** row shows the uniform-tube vowel. The rows **Mode 1 @ F1**, **Mode 2 @ F2** and **Mode 3 @ F3** separate its three displayed air-motion patterns.
The small blue circles represent groups of air molecules. The closed end is on the **left**, and the open lip end is on the **right**. Each row uses the same tract orientation.

teaching.text: A constriction at a strongly moving location tends to **lower that mode’s formant** because of added mass. A constriction where compression is strong tends to **raise it** because of added stiffness.
children: Near the closed end, motion is weak and compression is strong. Near the open lips, motion is strong and compression is weak.
**F1, F2 and F3** rank the air resonances from lowest to highest. The mode number identifies a pattern, while its formant gives the frequency associated with that pattern.

teaching.text: Both modes move strongly at the **lip end**. Inside the tube their patterns differ, so the same marked point can have strong motion in one mode and strong compression in the other.
children: The top and bottom rows show the **same air column** in modes 1 and 2, associated with the first and second formants, **F1 and F2**.

teaching.text: The modeled **/a/** constriction is near one third of the distance from the glottis, and **/i/** is near two thirds. **/u/** loads the lip end.
children: For each formant, the local movement decides how much added mass matters, and local compression decides how much added stiffness matters.
The **1/3** and **2/3** values locate points along the tract measured from the fixed glottal end. They are positions, while F1 and F2 name the resonances being affected.

explained: same air column in two modes

teaching.text: For **/u/**, lip rounding narrows the passage at the free end. The effective mass and stiffness of the air increase there.
children: The **larger blue masses at the right-hand end** show the added mass near the lips. The upper and lower rows apply that same change to **mode 1/F1** and **mode 2/F2**.

teaching.text: Both modes have **strong motion and little compression at the lips**. The added mass therefore slows both modes, while the added stiffness has little effect.
children: The prediction is **F1 down and F2 down**. A recording that moves from schwa into /u/ shows both formants dropping.
The downward arrows in **F1 ↓ and F2 ↓** mean both resonance frequencies decrease. They do not show air flowing downward; the air moves back and forth along the tract.

explained: same local change in two modes

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two thirds of the distance from the glottis**. The same narrowing raises both effective mass and stiffness there.
children: The **highlighted region around the 2/3 mark** locates the modified air in both rows. This fraction is distance from the glottis, while **mode 1/F1** and **mode 2/F2** identify the patterns being compared.

teaching.text: Mode 1 has strong motion at that location, so the added mass lowers **F1**. Mode 2 has strong compression and expansion there, so the added stiffness raises **F2**.
children: The recording from schwa into /i/ shows the predicted result, **F1 down and F2 up**.

In **F1 ↓ and F2 ↑**, the arrows mean the first resonance becomes lower in frequency and the second becomes higher. Both changes result from the same constriction, rather than two separate tongue movements.

teaching.text: The modeled **/a/** constriction is near **one third of the distance from the glottis**. Compression is strong there in mode 1, so added stiffness raises **F1**.
children: The **highlighted region near 1/3** is the changed location in both chains. The fraction measures distance from the fixed glottal end, not a third of the frequency.

teaching.text: Motion is strong there in mode 2, so added mass lowers **F2**.
children: The result is **F1 up and F2 down**. The two formants respond differently because the same location participates differently in their modes.

The upper chain shows **mode 1/F1** and the lower shows **mode 2/F2**. In **F1 ↑ and F2 ↓**, the arrows describe resonance frequency increases and decreases, rather than the direction in which air travels.

teaching.text: **Motion and compression alternate along the air column.** In one region, air travels strongly with little change in spacing. In another, the spacing changes strongly while local motion is small.
children: The top **Schwa** row shows the uniform-tube vowel. The rows **Mode 1 @ F1**, **Mode 2 @ F2** and **Mode 3 @ F3** separate its three displayed air-motion patterns.
The small blue circles represent groups of air molecules. The closed end is on the **left**, and the open lip end is on the **right**. Each row uses the same tract orientation.

teaching.text: Higher modes place those regions differently. A constriction can therefore fall in a moving region for one formant and a compressing region for another.
children: Predict the effect separately for each mode. Added moving mass lowers its frequency, while added stiffness where air compresses raises it.
**F1, F2 and F3** rank the air resonances from lowest to highest. The mode number identifies a pattern, while its formant gives the frequency associated with that pattern.

teaching.text: In **source-filter theory**, the **source** is vocal-fold vibration and the **filter** is the air in the vocal tract. They contribute different patterns to the same vowel sound.
children: The **left plot** is the source before filtering, and the **right plot** is the same source after the vocal tract changes the harmonic amplitudes. Frequency in **Hz** runs horizontally, and amplitude runs vertically in both.

teaching.text: The source supplies **harmonics**, the evenly spaced peaks at multiples of its base frequency. The tract’s **formants** determine which harmonics come through strongly.
children: Harmonics near a formant have greater amplitude, while those between formants have less amplitude.

**Harmonics every 100 Hz** means neighboring source peaks are 100 Hz apart, with a **base frequency, F0, of 100 Hz**. The labeled **F1 at 500 Hz** and **F2 at 1,500 Hz** mark air resonances, rather than the source’s first and second harmonics.

teaching.text: The **envelope** is the broad outline traced by the harmonic heights. Changing the vowel moves the formants and changes this outline.
children: With the source held fixed, the harmonic frequencies stay in place. Their **heights change** because the filter has changed.
The markers **F3 and F4** continue the ordering of higher air resonances. Their Hz values locate them on the same frequency axis as the harmonics, while peak height still indicates amplitude.

teaching.text: The **/i/** filter has a **low F1** and a **high F2**. Harmonics near those resonances become strong, leaving a wide gap between the two groups of tall peaks.
children: The **100 Hz spacing** belongs to the source harmonics in the left plot. In the filtered plot, **F1 at 300 Hz** and **F2 at 2,300 Hz** locate the first two /i/ resonances, far apart on the horizontal frequency axis.

teaching.text: The source’s harmonic frequencies stay the same. What changes is their **amplitude**, giving the envelope its /i/ pattern.
children: The widely separated formants agree with the modeled /i/ constriction, which lowers F1 and raises F2.
The two plots keep the **same source and harmonic positions**. Compare peak heights vertically to see the filter’s effect; a taller harmonic has greater amplitude, not greater frequency.

teaching.text: The **/a/** filter has a **higher F1** and a **lower F2**, placing the first two formants closer together. Harmonics near them become tall and form a broad low-frequency group.
children: The right plot labels **F1 at 750 Hz** and **F2 at 1,200 Hz**. These example resonance positions are closer together than the /i/ pair. The source still has harmonics spaced **100 Hz** apart.

teaching.text: The harmonics remain at the frequencies supplied by the source. The filter changes their **heights**, creating the envelope for /a/.
children: The formant positions agree with the modeled constriction that raises F1 and lowers F2.
Read **frequency in Hz horizontally** and **amplitude vertically**. The left and right plots use the same harmonic positions, so their changing peak heights isolate what the filter does.

teaching.text: A **spectrum** displays the frequencies and amplitudes in one short portion of sound. A **spectrogram** places successive spectra in time so that changing speech sounds can be followed.
children: The small panels labeled **spectrum 1, 2 and 3** show successive time samples of each vowel. Their numbers count moments, rather than the first three formants.

teaching.text: In the spectrogram, **time runs left to right**, **frequency runs bottom to top**, and **darkness shows amplitude**. Darker regions contain stronger energy.
children: A formant appears as a dark band because harmonics near that air resonance have high amplitude.

The gray key makes **high amplitude black**, medium amplitude gray and low amplitude white. The frequency scale is in **Hz**, meaning cycles per second; darker is stronger rather than higher in frequency.

teaching.text: During **/i/**, F1 is low and F2 is high, so the bands are far apart. Moving into **/a/** raises the low band and lowers the high band, bringing the formants closer together.
**Harmonics reveal formants through their amplitudes.** Closely spaced harmonics give many peaks around each formant, making its overall shape easier to identify.
children: The comparison holds the **vocal-tract filter fixed**, with example resonances **F1 at 300 Hz** and **F2 at 2,100 Hz**. Those are air-resonance frequencies, rather than harmonic spacing.

teaching.text: A higher **F0**, the base frequency of vocal-fold vibration, spreads the harmonics farther apart. Fewer peaks then fall near each formant, and a formant can lie between them.
children: Changing F0 does not by itself move the filter’s formants. It changes how densely the harmonics show their shape.
In the low-pitch case, **F0 = 100 Hz** gives harmonics 100 Hz apart. **F0 = 250 Hz** gives wider 250 Hz spacing. The inset also shows an even higher F0 of 350 Hz, with the same two formant regions.

teaching.text: This makes formants harder to identify in high-pitched voices, including those of toddlers and sopranos. A widely spaced harmonic can be mistaken for the formant region that strengthens it.
children: The toddler and soprano frequency lists illustrate the same effect with still wider harmonic spacing. They describe example source frequencies, rather than new formants created by a different vowel.

review.scope: Reviewed all61 source pages of Lectures11–13 against Original C Version2. Patches supply complete replacement teaching blocks; unpatched pages inherit that edition without alteration.
review.visualReview: All static source-page contact sheets and selected full-size figure panels were inspected. The15 distinct embedded videos were checked through frames at12%,47% and79% of duration during the preceding source review, and their original image assets and visible labels were rechecked for this edition. This is sampled visual review, not complete animation or audio playback. The harmonics/formants GIF has one frame and was inspected as a still image.
review.meaningfulValues: Retains values that identify a condition, location, axis, relative rate or resonance/source distinction. Does not recite every footnote ratio, playback setting or frequency label, and adds no worked calculation.
review.sourceCorrections: The printed L12 stiffness-down arrow remains untouched in the source visual and is explained as a typo in the new teaching. Membrane frequency values remain identified as assigned illustration settings rather than natural rectangle resonances.
